summary: We developed a gait foundation model from three-dimensional skeletal motion data of 3,328 deeply phenotyped adults, recorded using a depth camera during five motor tasks. Embeddings significantly predicted 1,887 of 3,210 phenotypic targets and provided predictive gains across all 18 body systems in men and 17 out of 18 in women, while also improving prediction of clinical diagnoses and medication use.
title: Deep learning-based gait analysis predicts multisystem health phenotypes

summary: Incretin mimetics as obesity therapy induce substantial weight and fat loss but also decrease lean soft tissue mass, possibly impairing skeletal muscle function. Here, in this two-arm randomized controlled trial of adding resistance exercise (REx) to tirzepatide (T), 120 adults with overweight or obesity were treated with tirzepatide and randomized to thrice-weekly resistance exercise training or usual activities for 40 weeks. Tirzepatide was safe, and most participants tolerated up-titration to 15 mg weekly. Adherence to resistance exercise was 91%. Weight loss achieved was similar (T = −22.61 kg, T+REx = −22.28 kg, P = 0.694). For primary outcomes, loss of total fat mass was similar (T = −17.19 kg, T+REx = −17.98 kg, P = 0.700; between-group difference = −0.77 kg, 95% confidence interval (CI): −2.14 kg to 0.60 kg), but resistance exercise reduced loss of total lean soft tissue mass (T = −4.67 kg, T+REx = −3.57 kg, P < 0.001; between-group difference = 1.09 kg, 95% CI: 0.43−1.75 kg). For related endpoints, resistance exercise reduced loss of appendicular lean soft tissue mass (T = −3.55 kg, T+REx = −2.92 kg, P < 0.001). Upper and lower body muscle strength decreased with tirzepatide (bench press −4.09 kg, lat pulldown −4.42 kg, knee extension −4.42 kg) but increased with T+REx (+4.68 kg, +8.58 kg, +5.88 kg, respectively, all P < 0.001 versus tirzepatide). In conclusion, resistance exercise training attenuated loss of total lean soft tissue mass, representing an effective adjunct to tirzepatide anti-obesity therapy. Australian New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry identifier: ACTRN12623001236684 . Participants undergoing resistance exercise while receiving tirzepatide lost less lean mass than participants receiving tirzepatide alone.
title: Resistance exercise to attenuate lean mass loss during tirzepatide therapy for obesity: a randomized controlled trial

summary: A barrier to precision medicine for ulcerative colitis (UC) is the inability to predict and mechanistically explain treatment responses. Using patient-reported outcomes (PROs) from a phase 3b comparative trial of 768 participants, we identified four distinct patient response-trajectory groups for vedolizumab (anti-integrin) and adalimumab (antitumor necrosis factor). Validation in a second phase 3 trial of 576 participants linked PRO-defined vedolizumab trajectories to long-term disease complications. Bulk, single cell, and spatial transcriptomics and proteomics identified vascular inflammation as associated with vedolizumab nonresponse through interactions between SPP1+ macrophages and endothelial cells. In two separate real-world cohorts of 4,981 and 3,854 patients with UC, concomitant use of renin–angiotensin system inhibitors (modulators of vascular inflammation) was associated with reduced long-term complications for vedolizumab but not anticytokine therapies. These findings define a response-trajectory-based taxonomy that requires prospective validation for clinical utility and applications for selecting vedolizumab combination therapy in UC. An analysis of patient-reported trajectories of response to vedolizumab in ulcerative colitis defines disease endotypes and identifies vascular inflammation as a potential resistance mechanism.
title: An ulcerative colitis taxonomy defined by individual patient-reported response trajectories

summary: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists improve symptoms in patients with obesity and heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF). We recently demonstrated that semaglutide reduces exertional pulmonary artery wedge pressure (PAWP) in obesity-related HFpEF, but potential effects of semaglutide on cardiac structure and function that may underlie these hemodynamic improvements remain unclear. In this prespecified cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) substudy of the randomized CAMEO-SEMA trial, 49 participants (33 semaglutide, 16 placebo, 28 female) underwent CMR at baseline and 52 weeks, within 1 day of invasive exercise hemodynamic assessment. The prespecified primary CMR endpoint was change in left atrial (LA) reservoir strain; other prespecified CMR endpoints included LV filling dynamics, which were assessed by early filling rate indexed to end-diastolic volume (eFR/EDV). Compared with placebo, semaglutide improved LA reservoir strain (+5.7% [95% CI, +0.3 to +9.7]; P=0.037) and eFR/EDV (+0.64 s−1 [95% CI, +0.42 to +1.00]; P<0.0001). Improvements in LA reservoir strain and LV filling dynamics were associated with reductions in exercise PAWP (r=−0.46, P<0.001 and r=−0.65, P<0.0001, respectively). With respect to other prespecified CMR endpoints, semaglutide reduced LV mass, restored more physiologic LV geometry, and improved right ventricular function and biventricular myocardial mechanics. The results of this CMR substudy indicate that in patients with obesity-related HFpEF, semaglutide improves LA function and LV diastolic filling dynamics, identifying improvements in myocardial function that may contribute to semaglutide’s improvement of hemodynamics. ClinicalTrials.gov number: NCT05371496. As presented at the 2026 AHA Scientific Sessions, a cardiac magnetic resonance substudy of the CAMEO-SEMA trial showed that semaglutide significantly improved cardiac structure and function, including left atrial reservoir strain and left ventricular filling dynamics, in individuals with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction and obesity.
title: Effects of semaglutide on cardiac structure and function in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction and obesity: a pre-specified cardiac magnetic resonance substudy of the CAMEO-SEMA trial

summary: The glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist semaglutide improves symptoms in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) through unclear mechanisms. Here, in this double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, we randomly assigned 81 patients (47 women) with HFpEF and obesity to semaglutide (2.4 mg weekly) or placebo for 52 weeks. The primary outcome was the change in invasively measured pulmonary artery wedge pressure (PAWP), a direct measure of cardiac congestion, during low-intensity exercise. Additional mechanistic outcomes included other hemodynamic measures and hemodynamic HFpEF remission (defined as normal PAWP under conditions of both rest and exercise at 52 weeks). At baseline, PAWP was 17.5 ± 4.3 mmHg at rest and 31.7 ± 5.2 mmHg during exercise. After 52 weeks, the mean change in PAWP during exercise was −9.8 (95% confidence interval (CI): −11.3 to −8.2) mmHg with semaglutide and +0.9 (95% CI: −1.3 to 3.0) mmHg with placebo (estimated difference, −10.6 mmHg; 95% CI: −13.3 to −8.0; P < 0.0001). As compared to placebo, semaglutide also decreased resting PAWP (estimated difference, −7.1 mmHg; 95% CI: −9.8 to −4.4; P < 0.0001), and semaglutide-treated patients were more likely to experience hemodynamic remission (53.7% versus 7.4%, odds ratio = 14.1, 95% CI: 3.0−134.6, P < 0.001). The results from this trial indicate that, in patients with HFpEF and obesity, treatment with semaglutide reduced left heart filling pressures during exercise and at rest and was associated with hemodynamic HFpEF remission in over half of treated patients. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT05371496 . As presented at the 2026 American Heart Association Scientific Sessions, in a placebo-controlled randomized clinical trial, semaglutide significantly improved pulmonary artery wedge pressure and other hemodynamic parameters during low-intensity exercise in individuals with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction and obesity.
title: Hemodynamic effects of semaglutide in individuals with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction and obesity: a placebo-controlled randomized clinical trial

summary: Gait is increasingly recognized as a vital sign, yet current approaches treat it as a symptom of specific pathologies rather than a systemic biomarker. Here we developed a gait foundation model for three-dimensional skeletal motion, which was recorded via a single-depth camera during 5 motor tasks, from 3,328 deeply phenotyped adults. Our purpose was to capture the full pattern of a person’s movement and use it to predict health phenotypes such as grip strength and sleep quality across 18 body systems. Gait is conventionally described by engineered features (for example, calculated measurements such as cadence and stride length), which may fail to capture the fine detail of how a person moves. Our model instead translates movement into learned embeddings: sets of numbers that describe how all body joints move together over time. Learned embeddings outperformed engineered features for prediction of age (Pearsonʼs r = 0.69), body mass index (r = 0.91) and visceral adipose tissue area (r = 0.83), and embeddings significantly predicted 1,887 of 3,210 tested phenotypes. Relative to a baseline model using age, body mass index, visceral adipose tissue and height alone, gait embeddings improved prediction in all 18 systems in males and 17 of 18 in females, as well as prediction of clinical diagnoses and medication use. Anatomical ablation analyses revealed that leg dynamics dominated metabolic and frailty predictions, and torso dynamics encoded sleep and lifestyle phenotypes. These findings establish gait as an independent, multisystem biosignal, motivating integration of gait analysis into routine clinical assessment as a scalable, passive vital sign. A gait foundation model, developed using three-dimensional skeletal motion data from 3,328 adults, predicts a wide array of clinical characteristics and diagnoses, including cardiometabolic, mental health and frailty phenotypes.
title: A gait foundation model for prediction of multisystem health phenotypes from 3D skeletal motion

summary: Digital health may extend cardiovascular care in communities with limited specialist access, but its effectiveness depends on whether communities have the infrastructure, devices, affordability, and capacity needed to use digital services. We linked national data on cardiometabolic disease burden, cardiology workforce, and digital readiness across 82,999 US census tracts. Among high-burden tracts in counties with no cardiologist or declining per-capita cardiologist supply, 4,765 (18.0%) tracts representing 19.9 million residents had higher digital readiness and were thus classified as deployment-priority tracts, whereas 21,752 (82.0%) tracts representing 74.1 million residents had lower readiness and were investment-priority tracts. Investment-priority tracts were spread across the urban-rural continuum and faced different barriers (adoption versus infrastructure). Contrasting classifications frequently occurred among neighboring census tracts within the same metropolitan area, highlighting geographic variation not captured by county-level targeting. Findings were broadly consistent across nine additional analyses with varying measures of readiness, workforce access, and classification thresholds. These findings provide a national framework for distinguishing communities where digital cardiovascular care may be deployed from those where infrastructure and adoption support may first be needed to enable equitable implementation. As presented at 2026 AHA Scientific Sessions: Analysis of U.S. Census and other national health data identifies communities with high cardiovascular care needs and assess health system readiness for digital care deployment.
title: Digital readiness for cardiovascular care in high-burden US communities with cardiology workforce constraints

summary: Analyses disentangling the role of the gut microbiome in linking lifestyle factors to health outcomes remain limited. Here, using fecal shotgun metagenomics from 6,803 adults in the Japanese 4D cohort, we identified two opposing microbiome-mediated axes linking lifestyle to health and 15 diseases. A health-associated axis enriched in microbial metabolism of dietary components was linked to plant-based, soy and dairy intake. In contrast, a disease-associated axis, enriched in oral-derived bacteria and pathobionts, was linked to refined carbohydrates and sedentary behavior. Starter culture microorganisms used to ferment foods did not show statistically significant mediation of the observed health effects. Alcohol was associated with both health- and disease-oriented mediation patterns involving microbial host-glycan utilization. Microbiome-defined health- and disease-oriented mediator axes were supported by fecal short-chain fatty acids and plasma cytokines from >1,700 individuals, revealing butyrate-associated anti-inflammatory and pro-inflammatory host profiles, respectively. Microbiome-based prediction (MADE) scores captured lifestyle–microbiome–disease mediation patterns and distinguished individual diseases across 13 independent external cohorts from the United States, China, Sweden, Russia and Australia. We identify the gut microbiome as a key mediator linking lifestyle to health and disease, providing a framework for microbiome-based assessment to guide lifestyle interventions for health promotion and disease prevention. Fecal shotgun metagenomics from 6,803 adults in the Japanese 4D cohort and microbiome-based prediction scores validated across 13 independent and geographically diverse cohorts revealed two opposing microbiome-mediated axes linking lifestyle to health and 15 diseases.
title: Opposing microbiome-mediated axes link modifiable lifestyles to health and chronic diseases
